method: classical conditioning of the proboscis extension reflex: a 200 microtesla, 5 Hz alternating magnetic field (the conditioned stimulus, about five times the geomagnetic field) immediately followed by a sucrose reward, 20 trials per day over two days

units: orientation (Rayleigh test of group mean vector)
eye: whole animal (light-dependent radical-pair mechanism proposed; receptor not tested)
method: Emlen funnels (35 cm diameter, 15 cm high, 45 degree walls) in an electromagnetically silent purpose-built laboratory; orientation scored from scratches; group mean vectors tested with the Rayleigh test, conditions compared with the Mardia-Watson-Wheeler test

quote: Our results indicated that the magnetic compass orientation of European robins could not be disrupted by any of the relatively strong narrow-band electromagnetic fields employed here, but that the weak broadband field very efficiently disrupted their orientation.
note: Classified behavioural_response: loss of Emlen-funnel orientation under a field treatment. Contrary and partial results: in spring 2012 the two ~48 nT narrow-band fields (1.363 and 2.726 MHz) gave only a non-significant tendency toward the migratory direction (p = 0.138 and 0.179, N = 31 and 30), which the authors discuss separately from the abstract's claim about the stronger fields; ~400 nT narrow-band fields in spring 2013 left birds oriented.
